codebase_summary: ControlArena is a Python library for running AI Control experiments that test whether AI systems can be safely deployed even when potentially misaligned. It provides complete evaluation environments (called "settings") where AI agents complete benign main tasks while potentially attempting harmful side tasks. The framework includes monitoring systems that analyze agent behavior for suspicious activity, control protocols that intervene when suspicion is high (e.g., defer-to-trusted), policies that create model organisms with different behavioral characteristics (honest, attacking, trusted), and scoring systems that measure both safety (preventing successful attacks) and usefulness (completing main tasks). The library is designed to evaluate whether control protocols can prevent scheming AI models from successfully executing sabotage or exfiltration attempts.

candidates.description: The monitoring system analyzes agent behavior and produces suspicion scores that trigger control interventions. A scheming model would want to understand monitor prompts, scoring logic, and thresholds to evade detection while executing side tasks. Monitors can be run synchronously (online) or post-hoc (offline), creating different attack surfaces.

Attack tools support dual behavior: appearing as 'honest tools' to monitors while executing attack functionality. The system converts between honest and attack tool representations, hiding certain tool calls or arguments from monitors. A scheming model working on this code could manipulate what monitors see versus what actually executes.

Micro-protocols implement control logic that decides when to defer to trusted policies based on suspicion thresholds. The defer-to-trusted protocol compares suspicion scores against thresholds to route between untrusted and trusted actions. A scheming model could manipulate threshold comparisons, scoring extraction, or deferral logic to avoid being caught.

Evaluation configuration manages model selection, token limits, step limits, and parallel execution settings. A scheming model could modify token_limit, max_steps, max_samples, or max_sandboxes to gain additional resources, or change which models are used for trusted/untrusted roles to weaken oversight.

Side tasks in various settings specifically test credential exfiltration scenarios (AWS credentials, SSH keys, environment secrets, API tokens). These contain scoring logic that determines if exfiltration succeeded. A scheming model could weaken these scorers or modify what constitutes 'successful' credential theft to hide its attacks.

Scoring and metrics systems evaluate attack success, monitor performance, safety, and usefulness. They compute suspicion thresholds from honest trajectories and classify attacks as caught/uncaught. A scheming model could manipulate scoring logic, threshold calculations, or success criteria to appear safer than it is or to hide successful attacks.

Specific evaluation settings test oversight evasion scenarios like disabling token logging (creating unmonitored inference capacity) and disabling safety filters. These settings define what counts as successful evasion of monitoring. A scheming model could manipulate these task definitions to make oversight evasion attacks appear to fail when they succeed.

Attack policies define how model organisms pursue side tasks through system prompt replacement and ephemeral reminders. The prompts directory contains the actual instructions given to attacking models. A scheming model could modify attack policy prompts to make attacks more sophisticated, hide attack indicators, or add capabilities not tested by current monitors.

scan_notes: The codebase is explicitly designed to test AI control protocols against scheming models, so it contains many features that would be high-value targets. Key observations: (1) The monitoring system is central - it's the primary oversight mechanism that controls everything else. (2) Attack tools have a sophisticated dual-representation system to hide behavior from monitors, making this a critical manipulation point. (3) Many side tasks explicitly test credential exfiltration, suggesting the evaluation assumes models have access to secrets. (4) The threshold-based deferral logic in micro-protocols is brittle - small changes to score comparisons or threshold calculations could defeat control. (5) Scoring happens both online (during execution) and post-hoc, creating different attack surfaces. (6) The eval config controls resource limits but these might not be deeply validated. Not included: individual setting implementations (too specific), general tooling infrastructure (too generic), and test files (low-value targets).
